children: The chapter ends with “Yes,” as it began. Here the “Yes” comes as a memory of sexual consent (during Molly’s first meeting with Leopold) and an affirmation of life, femininity, and sexuality. Joyce’s associations with “yes” were very specific: he called it “the female word,” “the least forceful word I could possibly find” to end the book, and wrote that it
“denotes acquiescence, self-abandon, relaxation, the end of all resistance.”
In the Linati schema, Joyce has the hour as
none
and the 8 sentences of the “Penelope” chapter represent infinity, i.e. the 8 on its side–or as Joyce biographer Richard Ellmann wrote eloquently:

The time is no o’clock, or as he said in an Italian schema of the book, it is the time indicated mathematically by the lemniscate or figure eight lying on its side—∞—the number of infinity and eternity. It might be more exact to say that the ruins of time and space coexist with the mansions of eternity and infinity, at least until the very end.

children: It’s interesting for Molly to call these the devil’s queer names since Gibraltar is in reference to the Spanish translation of the Arabic Jabal Ṭāriq, or Tariq ibn Ziyad, who led an army across the Gibraltar Strait . Delapaz was a Spanish religious suffix adopted by Jewish converts to Christianity, and paz which means “peace.” Gracia is spanish for “grace” or “mercy,” usually with Christian connotations. Calling these devilish names could be ironic, also fitting in with how Stephen rejects the Church. Dedalus also meaning “craftsman” could connect to Mary’s husband Joseph in the Bible who was a carpenter, perhaps making the devilish connection more contradictory.
